clue.text: Forebodings now I'm getting sent out

indicators.note: letters sent out are scattered, so the word before is rearranged

blocks.note: the present is now
taken as written
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone senses trouble ahead as they are being dispatched somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Presentiments are vague intuitive feelings that something unpleasant is about to happen, which is what forebodings are.

clue.text: Bewitching boy, obviously hipped, put in tights

definitions.text: Bewitching boy, obviously hipped, put in tights

blocks.clueFragment: Bewitching boy, obviously hipped, put in tights
blocks.note: surface reading: a captivating lad with curvy hips squeezed into hosiery
setter's reading: the hero of Cinderella in a pantomime, the principal boy, traditionally played by a shapely actress in tights

explanation.walkthrough: In British pantomime, the Christmas family stage show, the young male lead is played by a woman, hence the hips and the tights.
explanation.definitionFit: The charming royal suitor of Cinderella is the panto role most often given to an actress dressed as a young man.

clue.text: Cry up tenth item in sale, of Oriental type

indicators.note: Eastern scripts such as Arabic and Hebrew run right to left, so these letters are read backwards

blocks.note: E is short for East
each item at an auction is a lot
X is the Roman numeral for ten, numbering the tenth lot

explanation.surface: An auctioneer praises the tenth lot, an Eastern-style piece.
explanation.walkthrough: The tenth item is lot X, which written Eastern fashion, right to left, becomes XTOL; East's E goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry up is an old phrase for praising loudly, which is exactly what extolling means.

clue.text: Hence a stiff-necked generation of scholars?

definitions.text: Hence a stiff-necked generation of scholars?

blocks.clueFragment: Hence a stiff-necked generation of scholars?
blocks.note: surface reading: the reason a whole generation of pupils grew up proud and haughty
setter's reading: literally stiff at the neck, from the broad starched white collar worn by boys at a famous English public school

explanation.walkthrough: Stiff-necked usually means arrogant, a fair jibe at a famous English boarding school; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: This broad stiff white collar was part of the uniform worn by younger boys at that celebrated school near Windsor.

clue.text: Settler, broke, goes to Board for support

definitions.note: a trestle is not the board but the support under it

indicators.note: something broke is smashed, so its letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A penniless pioneer applies to the authorities for financial help.
explanation.walkthrough: Board for support reads like a welfare board; really it is a plank needing legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A trestle is a framework of legs and crossbar that holds up a tabletop or plank.

clue.text: School dames

blocks.note: surface reading: schoolmistresses, or the old village dame schools
setter's reading: the women who look after boarders' health and welfare at a boarding school

explanation.definitionFit: At British boarding schools the women in charge of pupils' health and laundry are traditionally given this title.

clue.text: The.usual stint by break of morn

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it apart, so the next word is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A labourer's ordinary daily stretch of work starting at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Break of morn looks like daybreak, but break is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is a standard quota of work expected, the usual amount set as a stint.

clue.text: Be silent, sauntering with awkward gait

blocks.note: the command for quiet
strolling at a leisurely pace

explanation.surface: A quiet walker drifts along with a clumsy step.
explanation.definitionFit: Shambling describes walking clumsily, dragging the feet in an ungainly manner.

clue.text: Just crusts for dinner?

blocks.note: surface reading: a meagre supper of nothing but scraps of crust
setter's reading: a loaf that is the entire meal by itself, split as a pun on a type of brown loaf

explanation.walkthrough: Read the first word of the answer as two: a loaf that makes up the whole meal.
explanation.definitionFit: It is brown bread baked from flour that keeps the entire grain, here punned as an entire dinner of loaf.

clue.text: Brief formal presentation to Green-but he's withdrawn

definitions.note: a clause describing the person the answer names

blocks.note: short form of introduction, a formal presentation of one person to another
vert is the heraldic word for green

explanation.surface: Someone is introduced to a Mr Green, who turns out to be shy.
explanation.walkthrough: Vert is heraldry's name for green, a frequent crossword stand-by.
explanation.definitionFit: An introvert is a shy, inward-looking person, someone withdrawn into themselves.

clue.text: The extent river water is used for punch

blocks.note: first meaning: the range or scope something covers
second meaning: a straight stretch of a river between bends

explanation.surface: Someone asks how much river water goes into a bowl of punch.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail about punch nods to a boxer's arm length, which is also measured by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both range or scope and a continuous navigable stretch of a river.

clue.text: For internal upset, crude oil in metric measure

indicators.note: something crude is unrefined, so the next word is used in a rough new order
one thing is placed inside another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
cc is cubic centimetre

explanation.surface: A dose of crude oil measured in millilitres as a remedy for indigestion.
explanation.walkthrough: Crude oil looks like petroleum, but crude is the instruction; the oil goes between the two Cs.
explanation.definitionFit: Colic is severe abdominal pain, a disorder of the stomach or bowels.

clue.text: You going to, the sands ? What a crowd !

indicators.note: the named part is departing and leaves the word

blocks.note: a crowd numbering thousands
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beach outing, and the shore is packed with people.
explanation.walkthrough: Thou is the old form of you; remove the sands from thousands.
explanation.definitionFit: Thou is the archaic singular form of the second-person pronoun, the old way of addressing someone directly.

clue.text: The second one a dam jointly fathered

definitions.text: The second one a dam jointly fathered

blocks.clueFragment: The second one a dam jointly fathered
blocks.note: surface reading: livestock breeding, a second offspring shared by a sire and a dam
setter's reading: join the two words to get the first man of Genesis, whose second son is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: A dam is a mother animal, which points the solver at breeding; run the words together.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the first couple had Cain first and then a younger brother, the shepherd Cain killed.

clue.text: Does this meths consumer show the ghost?

definitions.text: Does this meths consumer show the ghost?

blocks.clueFragment: Does this meths consumer show the ghost?
blocks.note: surface reading: a drinker of methylated spirits seeing apparitions
setter's reading: a small burner fuelled by methylated spirits, and a light to see a phantom by

explanation.walkthrough: Meths is British slang for methylated spirits, the fuel; spirit also means ghost.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit-lamp is a small burner that runs on alcohol fuel such as methylated spirits.

clue.text: One in Rachel's wild embrace is my darling

definitions.note: from the Jacobite song naming Bonnie Prince Charles as the singer's darling

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the name is set in a disordered arrangement
to embrace is to hold something within one's arms

blocks.note: the name, to be rearranged
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone held passionately in Rachel's arms is her beloved.
explanation.walkthrough: The old Scottish song is 'Charlie is my darling', so the clue quotes its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jacobite song title names Bonnie Prince Charlie as the singer's beloved, completing the familiar line.

clue.text: " Sternest " or greediest?

blocks.note: first meaning: furthest towards the stern of a ship
second meaning, split in two: after the most, wanting the largest share

explanation.walkthrough: Sternest looks like most severe, but it means nearest the stern; the second sense splits the answer into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Aftermost is the nautical term for furthest back in a ship, and read as two words means chasing the biggest portion.

clue.text: No good reason to soak him without a bob

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: to sop is to soak or dip in liquid
taken as written
a bob is a shilling, abbreviated s in old British money

explanation.surface: There is no proper excuse to drench a man who is penniless.
explanation.walkthrough: Without here means outside, not lacking. A bob was the slang name for a shilling, the pre-1971 coin abbreviated s.
explanation.definitionFit: A sophism is a clever but false argument, specious reasoning that does not hold up.

clue.text: Working on religious propaganda that should draw

blocks.note: to be at a task is to be working on it
a tract is a pamphlet of religious persuasion

explanation.surface: A writer of religious pamphlets hopes they will win followers.
explanation.definitionFit: To attract is to draw in or pull towards, as a magnet or a crowd-pleaser does.

clue.text: Barber of Bray

definitions.note: stands for the Vicar of Bray, the famous example of the answer

blocks.note: first meaning: one who cuts hair
second meaning: like the Vicar of Bray in the song, who switched beliefs under every new monarch to keep his post

explanation.surface: A hairdresser in a Berkshire village, echoing the Barber of Seville.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vicar of Bray, from an English folk song, kept his living by changing religion under each ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A trimmer is both someone who cuts hair and a political opportunist who shifts position to suit circumstances.

clue.text: Chilly-sounding place of Midas and the Mode

definitions.text: place of Midas and the Mode

blocks.note: surface reading: a place whose name sounds cold, like frigid or fridge

blocks.clueFragment: place of Midas and the Mode
blocks.note: setter's reading: the ancient kingdom in Asia Minor ruled by King Midas, which gave its name to a musical mode

explanation.walkthrough: The first syllable is pronounced like fridge, hence chilly.
explanation.definitionFit: King Midas ruled this ancient Anatolian kingdom, and the Phrygian mode in music is named after it.

clue.text: Rabelaisian of pagan addiction

blocks.note: Pan is the pagan Greek god of the wild
a craving or compulsion

explanation.surface: A bawdy character from Rabelais with a heathen craving.
explanation.definitionFit: Panurge is the roguish companion of Pantagruel in the comic novels of Rabelais.

clue.text: Sign of an illiterate gospeller. Jer?

blocks.note: first meaning: the cross someone who cannot write puts in place of a signature
second meaning: one of the four evangelists who wrote a Gospel
surface padding: a teasing abbreviation for the prophet Jeremiah, who wrote no Gospel

explanation.walkthrough: The trailing 'Jer?' teases with Jeremiah, a prophet who is not a gospeller.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the cross made instead of a signature and the evangelist of the second Gospel.

clue.text: Right of possession Though ye have - among the pots

definitions.text: Though ye have - among the pots

blocks.note: first meaning: a legal right to hold another's property until a debt is paid

blocks.clueFragment: Though ye have - among the pots
blocks.note: second meaning: the missing word from Psalm 68 in the King James Bible, an old past participle of lie

explanation.walkthrough: The verse runs 'Though ye have ___ among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a legal claim to retain property against a debt, and also the archaic participle of lie in the psalm.

clue.text: Tom the hitch-hiker?

definitions.note: completes a name rather than meaning it: Tom ___ of the fairy tale

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of the tiny hero of an English fairy tale
second meaning: the digit a hitch-hiker holds out, the question mark flagging the stretch

explanation.surface: A man called Tom standing at the roadside hoping for a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom completes the name of the miniature folk hero; hitch-hikers signal with this digit.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitch-hikers raise this digit to ask for a lift, and it completes the name of the miniature folk hero.

clue.text: A guru, but in part a South American bird

indicators.note: only a portion of the following words is used, a run of letters within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the words

explanation.surface: A spiritual teacher is, after all, partly a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The urubu is the black vulture of South and Central America.

clue.text: Man that Carl's associated with

blocks.note: first meaning: the island in the Irish Sea
second meaning: the word that follows Carl to make the name of a city in Cumbria

explanation.walkthrough: Man is the Isle of Man; Carlisle is a city in north-west England near the Scottish border.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is an island, and the word joined to Carl makes the English border city.

clue.text: No., all rights are cornered in them

definitions.note: a clause describing places, standing for the plural noun

blocks.note: the abbreviation for number, taken as written
OK means all right, and OKs is its plural

explanation.surface: A numbered set of approvals tucked away in corners.
explanation.definitionFit: Nooks are small recesses or corners, places where things are tucked away.

clue.text: Namely, a thousand to equip a lord for battle

definitions.note: the answer is a man's first name

blocks.note: Roman numeral for a thousand
to arm is to equip with weapons
taken as written
a duke is a high-ranking nobleman
completes the sense of equip, making clear it means supplying weapons

explanation.surface: That is to say, a thousand soldiers are raised to fit out a nobleman for war.
explanation.walkthrough: Namely usually means that is to say; here it is read as name-ly, of a forename.
explanation.definitionFit: Marmaduke is an old English male forename, so the answer is a name, as the cryptic sense of the definition suggests.

clue.text: Mouldy money? Or can we grow-it?

definitions.text: Mouldy money? Or can we grow-it?

blocks.note: surface reading: banknotes gone green with mould
setter's reading: the special exchange rate used for farm prices under the European Common Agricultural Policy

explanation.walkthrough: In the 1970s the 'green' rate converted EEC farm support prices into sterling, hence money linked to things grown.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the special sterling exchange rate set for agricultural payments under the European Community's farm policy.
